extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: examining best mode and claim definiteness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for compliance with the best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. 112) and for determining whether claim language is definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph. Includes claim interpretation rules (broadest reasonable interpretation), means‑plus‑function analysis, and thresholds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement (separate from enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode provision of 35 U.S.C. 112 is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement; if the applicant knew of a specific mode thought to be the best way to carry out the invention, the applicant has an obligation to disclose that information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Newton and Spectra‑Physics v. Coherent. The enablement requirement places the subject matter of the claims in the possession of the public generally; best mode requires disclosure of specific instrumentalities or techniques recognized by the applicant as the best way of carrying out the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Requirement to Update Best Mode for Foreign Priority/119(e)/120
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement to update the best mode in the context of a foreign priority application under 35 U.S.C. 119 or in applications claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: Standard Oil Co. v. Montedison and MPEP § 2165, subsection II. The disclosure in the earlier filed application must be made in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, other than the requirement to disclose the best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Cannot Be Cured by New Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If the best mode contemplated by the inventor at the time of filing is not disclosed, the defect cannot be cured by submitting an amendment adding that mode after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an amendment should be treated as new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251 and should be objected to and coupled with a requirement to cancel the new matter. Cites In re Hay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume Best Mode Disclosed Unless Evidence to Contrary
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should assume that the best mode is disclosed in the application unless evidence is presented that is inconsistent with that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode rejections in ex parte prosecution are extremely rare because the information necessary to form the basis for such a rejection is rarely accessible to the examiner and is generally uncovered in inter partes proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑Component Best Mode Analysis (Chemcast approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) a subjective inquiry whether the inventor at the time of filing knew of a mode considered better than any other; (B) an objective inquiry whether the disclosure is adequate to enable one skilled in the art to practice the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only if (A) is satisfied should the examiner analyze (B). A best mode rejection is proper only when the first inquiry (inventor knew of a preferred mode) is affirmative and the second inquiry (disclosure adequate) is negative, with reasons supporting non‑enablement of the best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of Concealment Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining adequacy of best mode disclosure, only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is to be considered; such evidence must tend to show the quality of disclosure is so poor as to effectively result in concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples: satisfies best mode where information missing but routine skill suffices (In re Sherwood, Honeywell, W.L. Gore, Scripps Clinic/Amgen). Violations where preferred method details not disclosed and not in prior art (Spectra‑Physics; Dana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement vs. Best Mode Distinction for Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A failure to set forth any mode is equivalent to nonenablement; best mode is distinct and focuses on whether inventor disclosed the particular mode he considered best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application sets forth no mode at all, that is an enablement problem (In re Glass). But where a specific preferred technique exists, best mode requires disclosure even if performance steps are known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Separate Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute sets forth two separate requirements: (A) claims must set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (subjective); (B) claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (objective/definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should determine whether a rejection under 112(b) is based on indefiniteness or on failure to claim what the inventor regards as the invention; see In re Zletz and Ex parte Ionescu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Definiteness Purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of definiteness is to ensure the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement; secondary purpose is to provide a clear measure of what applicants regard as the invention for patentability and 112(a) analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph. Rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants Are Their Own Lexicographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define terms in the claims in whatever terms they choose, provided any special meaning assigned to a term is clearly set forth in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language, alternative expressions, negative limitations, etc., are permissible if the special meaning is clearly set forth in the specification. Applicant may not add a special definition or disavowal after the filing date, but may point out a definition contained in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) During Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified. Words must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification; the specification is the best source for claim term meaning. See Yamamoto, Zletz, Buszard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine Whether Each Claim Limitation Invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA sixth paragraph); if so, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 for detailed means‑plus‑function analysis. This affects claim construction and scope during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Whether Claim Language is Definite (Threshold Requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner's focus is whether the claim meets statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision; a claim is indefinite if, given its BRI, a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claim terms in view of (A) the application disclosure, (B) prior art teachings, and (C) the understanding of a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Do not conflate breadth with indefiniteness: broad claims can be definite if boundaries are clear. Cite Packard, Zletz, Nautilus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Under Examination vs Patented Claims (Court Standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed differently during examination than in court; the PTO uses BRI during prosecution, while courts apply Nautilus's 'reasonable certainty' standard to issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should apply BRI to facilitate narrowing/amending during prosecution; applicants can amend claims during prosecution to ensure clarity. Persistent ambiguity after a well‑grounded rejection justifies a §112(b) rejection (Packard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed Essential Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential to the invention as described in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as not enabling; failure to interrelate essential elements may be rejected under 112(b) for failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. Case citations: In re Mayhew, In re Venezia, In re Collier. Note precedents holding interdependency not always required (Ex parte Nolden, Ex parte Huber).
